sub_answers.sub_question: What are known robustness and generalization limits of neural detectors when deployed under distribution shift or unseen impulsive interference?
sub_answers.text: Bayesian AMP–based detectors achieve exact analytical characterization of performance in the large-system limit only under certain assumptions on the MIMO system matrix and constellation alphabet, which limits their robustness under distribution shift or unseen interference [d47196s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How do sample complexity and identifiability bounds constrain learning unknown noise models in MIMO detection?
sub_answers.text: Ill-posed blind recovery problems become tractable when unknown inputs are constrained to lie in known low-dimensional subspaces, yielding exact recovery guarantees that imply identifiability requires such structural constraints [d58777s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What adversarial, stability, or safety concerns arise when ML detectors operate in safety-critical or regulated communication systems?
sub_answers.text: Rate-splitting strategies improve robustness to imperfect CSI, highlighting that detector vulnerability to CSI errors is a key stability concern in regulated or safety-critical systems [d58875s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What open theoretical lower bounds exist on detection error or capacity loss in presence of impulsive noise for data-driven versus model-based detectors?
sub_answers.text: Algorithms with provable optimality conditions in the large-system limit serve as benchmarks for detection error, as AMP-based detectors can achieve the same error-rate performance as individually optimal detectors under their assumptions, establishing lower-bound references for model-based methods [d47196s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How does improved impulsive-noise handling affect throughput, bit-error rate, and latency in wireless communication systems?
sub_answers.text: Improved impulsive-noise handling yields drastically lower bit-error rates in OFDM systems affected by impulsive interference [d19014s0p0]. Improved bit-error performance enables higher effective throughput through fewer retransmissions and better use of spectral-efficiency mechanisms [d32166s0p0]. Near-optimal impulsive-noise receivers can approach within 1 dB of the matched-filter bound, improving reliability at given SNRs [d19014s0p0]. Algorithms with O(N log N) complexity that are parallelizable can keep processing latency low enough for practical OFDM implementations [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What are computational complexity, power, and latency requirements of ML-based detectors compared with classical algorithms in real-time MIMO receivers?
sub_answers.text: Maximum-likelihood detection has complexity that grows exponentially with spectral efficiency, making it computationally intensive for real-time receivers [d140430s0p0]. Advanced detectors that combine lattice and list principles can achieve near-ML performance with more efficient, parallelizable implementations, reducing computational load [d140430s0p0]. Iterative and residual-based algorithms (e.g., MINRES, GMRES, CR) substantially cut complexity and thus power and latency compared with exact matrix inversion, with reported complexity reductions up to about 87% in massive MIMO scenarios [d42417s0p0]. Algorithms designed for large MIMO based on approximate message passing can be computationally efficient while approaching optimal error rates under suitable assumptions, offering favorable real-time trade-offs [d47196s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How have learning-based detectors been validated in practical settings such as cellular, Wi-Fi, or radar systems?
sub_answers.text: Detectors and receivers for impulsive-noise and MIMO scenarios have been validated primarily via numerical simulations and BER analyses in OFDM, powerline, and Wi‑Fi relevant settings [d19014s0p0]. MIMO-UWOC systems and MIMO-OFDM-IM receivers have been evaluated through analytical BER expressions confirmed by photon-counting simulations and extensive computer simulations respectively [d28843s0p0][d32166s0p0]. Novel algorithms show simulation-based performance gains versus conventional linear detectors such as MMSE in OFDM and coded modulation contexts [d140430s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What defines impulsive noise and how does it differ statistically from Gaussian noise in communications?
sub_answers.text: Impulsive noise consists of uncoordinated interference events that are much stronger than thermal noise and occur sporadically [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What classes of learning-based detectors (e.g., neural nets, deep learning, hybrid models) are used in MIMO detection?
sub_answers.text: Deep neural networks and data-driven deep learning approaches are used for MIMO tasks such as precoding and detection [d71672s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What are commonly cited empirical benefits of ML-based detectors versus classical detectors under non-Gaussian noise?
sub_answers.text: Learning-based detectors can approach near-optimal performance while reducing computational complexity compared with traditional optimization, achieving close-to-optimal performance in practical inference phases [d71672s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What benchmark datasets and simulation scenarios are used to evaluate detector performance under impulsive noise?
sub_answers.text: Evaluations under impulsive or non-Gaussian noise use simulated scenarios such as OFDM transmissions with impulsive noise across N tones and compare against matched-filter bounds in simulation studies [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How do robust loss functions and heavy-tailed likelihood models (e.g., alpha-stable, mixture models) represent impulsive noise?
sub_answers.text: Robust losses can be formed by maximizing a kernel-based estimate of the residual density, i.e., by maximizing an estimated log-likelihood that coincides with MSE under Gaussian errors but remains stable under heavy-tailed noise [d115559s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What architectures and training strategies (e.g., model-based deep unfolding, autoencoders, RNNs) are used for MIMO detection?
sub_answers.text: Data-driven neural detectors using rectifier linear unit (ReLU) networks are used for MIMO detection and can asymptotically approach the MAP detector given sufficient training data [d67352s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How do parameter estimation methods (e.g., EM, variational inference, robust estimation) learn unknown noise distributions from data?
sub_answers.text: Joint parameter estimation is achieved by factor-graph message passing that jointly estimates channel coefficients, noise impulses, transmitted symbols, and bits using GAMP combined with forward-backward and turbo decoding [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How do feature representations and input preprocessing (e.g., pilot-based estimation, denoising) enable detectors to separate signal from impulsive disturbances?
sub_answers.text: Joint estimation approaches on factor graphs treat channel coefficients and noise impulses as latent variables to be inferred simultaneously with symbols, enabling separation of signal and impulsive disturbances through iterative message passing [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What theoretical results exist on universal approximation or consistency of neural detectors under model mismatch or heavy-tailed noise?
sub_answers.text: Data-driven DL detectors can asymptotically approach the MAP detector given sufficiently many training samples, establishing a form of consistency under ample data [d67352s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which documented robustness failures, generalization breakdowns, or calibration degradations occur for learned neural detectors when facing covariate shift, out-of-distribution impulsive interference, or heavy-tailed noise (e.g., alpha-stable or Middleton models), and what empirical or certified robustness margins have been reported?
sub_answers.text:
Deep models exhibit clear degradation under covariate shift when applied to unseen environments, causing reduced performance and calibration issues in batch-normalization based approaches [d70939s0p0].
Instance-wise customization of randomized-smoothing noise can significantly improve certified robustness margins such as average certified radius (ACR) and clean accuracy compared to universal-noise approaches [d65747s0p0].
Randomized-smoothing certification schemes can combine certificates from different noise distributions to improve certified robustness across multiple perturbation norms, yielding measurable ACR improvements [d84731s0p0].
Receivers designed for impulsive-noise OFDM environments can drastically outperform prior receivers and come within approximately 1 dB of the matched-filter bound, indicating empirical robustness margins against impulsive interference [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What formal sample complexity, PAC or minimax rates, and identifiability conditions have been derived for learning unknown impulsive-noise models in MIMO detection (including blind estimation settings), and how do Fisher-information/Cramér–Rao or latent-variable identifiability results constrain consistent recovery of noise parameters and detector performance?
sub_answers.text:
Joint bit-error-rate optimal receivers for OFDM under impulsive noise jointly estimate channel coefficients, noise impulses, finite-alphabet symbols, and unknown bits, which frames the estimation as a coupled inference problem rather than separate subproblems [d19014s0p0].
Near-optimal tractable algorithms based on loopy belief propagation and GAMP provide practical joint estimation with O(N log N) complexity, implying sample-complexity and computational tractability benefits for large-N systems [d19014s0p0].
De-biased GMM estimators can achieve parametric rates of convergence for robustness metrics under covariate shift, suggesting that semiparametric techniques yield formal rates in related estimation problems [d72663s0p0].
Local k-nearest-neighbour estimators for heavy-tailed designs achieve provable convergence rates that depend on tail-exponent conditions, indicating identifiability and sample-complexity sensitivities to tail behavior of the input distribution [d92663s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which adversarial risks, stability failure modes, regulatory or safety concerns, and documented attack vectors (e.g., spoofing, targeted impulse bursts, distributional poisoning) are associated with deploying ML-based detectors in safety-critical or regulated communication systems (automotive V2X, avionics, medical telemetry), and what mitigation, monitoring, or certification practices have been proposed?
sub_answers.text:
Adversarial examples are documented security threats for neural-network-based systems in safety-critical domains such as face recognition and self-driving cars, motivating certified-robustness approaches [d88466s0p0].
Randomized-smoothing based certification and training schemes have been proposed to mitigate adversarial risks by providing statistical guarantees on robustness at runtime [d88466s0p0].
Test-time normalization approaches can potentially deteriorate discriminative structures when source and target batch statistics mismatch, creating a failure mode relevant to monitoring and deployment in safety-critical systems [d70939s0p0].
Instance-wise and combined-noise certification strategies have been proposed as mitigation practices to improve robustness across multiple perturbation bounds and operating conditions [d65747s0p0][d84731s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What proven lower bounds or converse results (information-theoretic, minimax, or error-exponent bounds) exist for detection error rates or capacity loss under impulsive/heavy-tailed noise, and how do these bounds differ for data-driven (learned) detectors versus model-based detectors across classes of impulsive-noise channels?
sub_answers.text:
Factor-graph based receivers for impulsive-noise OFDM operate within about 1 dB of the matched-filter bound, providing an empirical converse benchmark on achievable performance under impulsive interference [d19014s0p0].
Randomized-smoothing certification provides provable certified radii (e.g., improvements in ACR) which act as lower bounds on the magnitude of adversarial perturbations that can be tolerated by smoothed classifiers [d84731s0p0].
De-biased GMM achieves parametric convergence rates for certain robustness metrics under covariate shift, establishing formal convergence lower bounds in semiparametric settings [d72663s0p0].
Generalization bounds for heavy-tailed SGD have been proven via Wasserstein stability for heavy-tailed SDEs and their discretizations, which constrain achievable error rates in heavy-tailed optimization regimes [d82558s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Quantify how robust mitigation of impulsive noise (e.g., alpha-stable interference, bursty PLC spikes) changes achievable throughput, packet error rate and symbol/bit-error-rate, and end-to-end latency in wireless links under various SNR/SIR and mobility scenarios; include metrics for link-layer retransmissions and QoS classes.
sub_answers.text:
Learning-based receivers that jointly estimate channel, noise impulses, symbols and bits can drastically reduce bit-error-rate under impulsive noise compared to conventional receivers [d19014s0p0].
A factor-graph-based receiver that merges GAMP with forward-backward and turbo decoding approaches can operate within about 1 dB of the matched-filter bound while drastically outperforming existing receivers in impulsive-noise OFDM settings [d19014s0p0].
Allowing retransmissions at the link layer can recover throughput for decoded-in-outage messages and can enable constrained optimal throughput to reach the unconstrained optimum depending on network density and error-rate constraints [d38456s0p0].
All-optical regenerative relaying that performs symbol-level discrimination avoids O/E/O conversion and thereby reduces end-to-end latency compared to decode-and-forward relays while suppressing noise accumulation seen in amplify-and-forward relays, improving reliability in multi-hop links under impulsive or implementation-dependent decision noise [d129041s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Compare runtime complexity (ops/second, MACs, parameter count), energy consumption (mW per inference or Joules per symbol), and inference latency (µs–ms) of ML-based MIMO detectors (CNNs, RNNs, Transformers, unfolded algorithms) versus classical detectors (ZF, MMSE, sphere decoding, message passing) when implemented on realistic hardware targets (DSPs, FPGAs, NPUs, CPUs).
sub_answers.text:
A factor-graph-based impulsive-noise OFDM receiver can be implemented with O(N log N) computational complexity and supports parallelization, reducing runtime relative to non-parallelizable iterative schemes [d19014s0p0].
One-bit precoding for frequency-selective massive MIMO is NP-hard, and block-wise processing incurs high computational complexity and processing delay compared to more efficient symbol-wise processing approaches [d83874s0p0].
Symbol-wise processing can significantly reduce processing delay and complexity versus block-wise processing while providing improved interference handling at the symbol rate [d83874s0p0].
Delay-Doppler domain THP for MU-MIMO-OTFS can be implemented without matrix decomposition or inversion, yielding a simple implementation that avoids heavy computation required by conventional precoding schemes [d82093s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Survey methods used to validate learning-based detectors in real deployments: over-the-air trials in 4G/5G base stations, Wi‑Fi testbeds, automotive or airborne radar experiments, and industry field trials; report measured gains/losses in BER, throughput, robustness, and deployment constraints observed in those settings.
sub_answers.text:
Link-level evaluations and simulations have been used to validate learning-informed physical-layer schemes, with link-level evaluations confirming throughput benefits of RSMA over SDMA and NOMA in downlink multi-antenna settings [d58875s0p0].
Monte Carlo simulations and numerical integration have been used to verify analytical performance of all-optical regenerative relays and to validate derived per-hop and end-to-end symbol error rate expressions under realistic impairments [d129041s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Detail practical data requirements and acquisition strategies for training ML MIMO detectors: dataset sizes (hours or number of channel realizations), supervised labeling approaches (pilot-aided labels, soft labels from high-complexity decoders, self-supervised/contrastive schemes), and recommended pilot patterns, SNR variations, and channel sounding designs needed to generalize across frequency bands, mobility and hardware impairments.

sub_answers.text: MIMO systems use multiple transmit and/or receive antennas to enable spatial multiplexing and/or diversity gains in wireless communications [d5873s0p0]. Channel estimation, detection (including maximum likelihood detection), and beamforming are canonical signal-processing tasks in MIMO receivers [d59366s0p0][d140430s0p0][d37453s0p0]. MIMO detection can have exponential complexity with spectral efficiency, motivating list and lattice decoding methods and novel detectors that seek reduced complexity while approaching ML performance [d140430s0p0]. Practical algorithmic challenges for these tasks include high computational complexity and latency, channel estimation errors and pilot contamination, inter-user and inter-cell interference, and other channel nonidealities that require robust transceiver and beamforming designs [d140430s0p0][d68195s0p0][d37453s0p0].

How are impulsive noise processes mathematically modeled using robust loss functions and heavy-tailed likelihoods — e.g., how do Huber/Tukey/M-estimators, alpha-stable distributions (with tail index α, skewness β, scale γ), Student-t, and Gaussian-mixture likelihoods represent outliers/impulses in the observation model, and what are the explicit forms of the corresponding negative-log-likelihoods and influence functions used for inference?
sub_answers.text: Huber-type losses downweight large residuals by switching from quadratic to linear penalty for outliers, producing robustness to heavy tails in factor and regression models [d84229s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which neural and hybrid architectures and training protocols have been proposed for MIMO symbol detection under non-Gaussian noise — for example, model-based deep unfolding variants (DetNet, OAMP-Net2, AMP-trained networks), LISTA-type unrolled solvers, autoencoder-based end-to-end receivers, and RNN/LSTM/GRU detectors — and what loss functions, supervision schemes (supervised, self-supervised, curriculum learning), and initialization strategies are reported to improve convergence and robustness?
sub_answers.text: A factor-graph receiver for OFDM in impulsive noise merges generalized approximate message passing (GAMP) with a forward–backward algorithm and soft-input soft-output decoding in a turbo loop to jointly estimate channel, impulses, symbols and bits [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What concrete parameter-estimation techniques are used to learn unknown impulsive-noise laws from data — e.g., EM for Gaussian-mixture and alpha-stable mixture models, fractional lower-order moments and characteristic-function fitting for stable laws, variational Bayes approximations, MCMC samplers, method-of-moments, and robust M-estimators (and their numerical solvers) — and what are their sample-complexity, convergence properties, and practical heuristics for identifiability?
sub_answers.text: Kernel-based robust losses learn noise characteristics by estimating the residual density and maximizing the estimated log-likelihood, thereby adapting to non-Gaussian errors [d115559s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which input feature constructions and preprocessing pipelines help detectors separate desired MIMO signals from impulsive disturbances — specifically, how are pilot-aided channel and noise-parameter estimation, matched filtering, time/frequency-domain blanking or clipping, median/wavelet denoising, short-time Fourier or cyclostationary features, and learned front-ends (convolutional denoisers, autoencoder encoders) used in practice, and what are the measured gains in BER or detection probability?
sub_answers.text: A joint factor-graph receiver estimates propagation channel coefficients and noise impulses together with symbols and bits, enabling separation of desired signals from impulsive disturbances in OFDM reception [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What rigorous theoretical guarantees (e.g., universal approximation, consistency, breakdown point, asymptotic efficiency, and generalization bounds) exist for neural or hybrid detectors operating under model mismatch or heavy-tailed/no-GLM noise — including results on approximation capacity of unrolled networks, statistical consistency under alpha-stable or mixture noise, robustness margins, and PAC-Bayes or Rademacher-complexity-style bounds that quantify performance degradation with heavy tails?
sub_answers.text: Huber-based tensor and factor estimators are provably consistent for estimating common factors and loading spaces under heavy-tailed distributions and remain robust even when only the second moment exists [d84229s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Under realistic distribution shifts and rare high-energy interference (e.g., alpha-stable impulsive noise, electromagnetic bursts, or nonstationary clutter), what empirical and theoretical limits have been reported on the robustness and out-of-distribution generalization of neural network–based signal detectors (including metrics like AUC, BER, EER, calibration, and worst-case error)?
sub_answers.text: A factor-graph-based receiver for OFDM in impulsive noise approaches within 1 dB of the matched-filter bound in bit-error-rate performance under impulsive noise conditions [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What are proven or empirically observed sample complexity bounds, identifiability conditions, or parameter-estimation rates for learning unknown additive or multiplicative noise distributions in MIMO detection (e.g., blind estimation of impulsive noise tails, mixture noise models, or heavy-tailed interference) and how do these limits scale with number of antennas, SNR, and model class complexity?
sub_answers.text: A probabilistic domain-generalization framework (Quantile Risk Minimization) comes with an empirical algorithm (EQRM) and a proven generalization bound for domain shifts under its meta-distribution assumptions [d77890s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which adversarial, stability, certification, or regulatory-safety failure modes have been documented for machine-learning detectors deployed in safety-critical or regulated comms (e.g., avionics, automotive V2X, medical telemetry)—including examples of targeted input perturbations, distributional adversaries, failure-to-detect events, and requirements for interpretable or certifiable behavior under standards?
sub_answers.text: Hallucination in large ASR models has been linked to dangerous failures in healthcare, legal, and aviation contexts, identifying a failure mode where low standard error metrics can conceal hazardous fabricated outputs [d105436s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What provable lower bounds or impossibility results exist comparing detection error floors, achievable information rates, or capacity degradation under impulsive/heavy-tailed noise for data-driven (learned) detectors versus classical model-based detectors (e.g., bounds based on minimax risk, Fano-type inequalities, or channel capacity loss under alpha-stable noise)?
sub_answers.text: A factor-graph-based receiver for impulsive-noise OFDM achieves performance within 1 dB of the matched-filter bound, providing an empirical upper-performance benchmark under impulsive noise that learned detectors can approach [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Quantitatively, what impact does robust mitigation of impulsive noise (e.g., alpha-stable, Middleton, or bursty interference) have on achievable throughput (Mbps), symbol/bit-error rates, and one-way/round-trip latency in OFDM and single-carrier wireless links under varying SNR and interference burst lengths?
sub_answers.text: A factor-graph-based OFDM receiver that jointly estimates channel, impulses, symbols, and bits drastically outperforms existing receivers under impulsive noise and achieves bit-error-rate performance within 1 dB of the matched-filter bound [d19014s0p0]. The proposed receiver has computational complexity that scales as O(N log N) for N tones and is amenable to parallelization, which constrains processing latency growth with system size [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: For real-time MIMO receivers, how do ML-based detection architectures (e.g., deep neural detectors, learned AMP, unfolding networks) compare to classical algorithms (e.g., MMSE, sphere decoding, belief propagation) in terms of computational complexity (ops/bit or ops/symbol), power consumption (mW per antenna or per GOPS), and processing latency (µs–ms) when implemented on typical hardware (DSP, FPGA, ASIC, mobile SoC)?
sub_answers.text: The proposed loopy belief-propagation approach merges GAMP with forward-backward and turbo decoding to yield a near-optimal algorithm with O(N log N) complexity and parallelizable structure, indicating favorable implementation complexity versus exhaustive ML approaches [d19014s0p0]. One-bit precoding in massive MIMO is NP-hard and block-wise processing (BWP) incurs high computational complexity and processing delay, whereas symbol-wise processing (SWP) can reduce complexity and latency while addressing ISI if designed to provide constructive interference for subsequent symbols [d83874s0p0]. Classical linear algorithms such as MMSE and iterative PMSE approaches trade complexity for near-optimal throughput, with simplified PMSE iterations providing near-optimal performance at reduced computational cost relative to full PDetMSE minimization [d4001s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What field demonstrations, testbed experiments, or standard-compliant trials have evaluated learning-based MIMO detectors in real-world systems (LTE/5G gNB/UE, Wi‑Fi 6/7 APs and clients, automotive or airborne radar), and what performance gains or limitations were observed across metrics like BLER, throughput, robustness to channel nonidealities, and regulatory/compatibility constraints?

When preparing ML detectors for deployment in operational MIMO links, what are the practical dataset needs (number of frames/snapshots, SNR/Doppler/channel state coverage), labeling strategies (supervised labels, self-supervision, synthetic vs. measured), and pilot/control-channel designs (pilot density, pilot power, pilot pattern) required to reach target detection performance and to generalize across channel conditions?
sub_answers.text: A DFT-spread OFDM design that inserts frequency-domain reference symbols can enable a low-complexity receiver to remove interference caused by puncturing and thus remove an error floor, illustrating that pilot/reference-symbol design can materially affect receiver error performance [d40112s0p0]. Algorithms for synchronization and channel estimation for turbo-coded MIMO-OFDM systems can be implemented on programmable hardware with significant scope for parallel processing, indicating practical implementability considerations for training/estimation procedures on real platforms [d41102s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Describe multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) communications from a signal-processing perspective: key system components (transmit/receive antennas, channel matrix, spatial streams), main estimation/detection tasks (channel estimation, symbol detection, equalization), and the principal technical challenges (inter-stream interference, channel fading/estimation errors, complexity and latency constraints).
sub_answers.text: MIMO systems employ multiple transmit and multiple receive antennas to provide multiplexing and/or diversity gains through spatial streams [d5873s0p0]. The propagation between transmit and receive arrays is represented by a channel matrix that couples spatial streams and must be estimated at the receiver [d5873s0p0]. Key signal-processing tasks include channel estimation, symbol detection (maximum-likelihood or suboptimal detectors), and equalization to separate spatial streams and recover transmitted symbols [d140430s0p0][d4001s0p0]. Principal technical challenges are inter-stream interference from multiplexed spatial streams, channel fading and imperfect CSI that degrade detection, and the computational complexity and latency of near-ML detection and joint estimation/detection algorithms [d4001s0p0][d90654s0p0][d140430s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Provide a precise operational definition of impulsive noise in digital communications, list common statistical models (e.g., Middleton class A/B, alpha-stable, Bernoulli-Gaussian), and explain how their probability tails, variance behavior, and higher-order statistics differ from the Gaussian noise assumption used in conventional receiver design.

Catalog the major categories of learning-based MIMO detectors reported in the literature, giving representative architectures and examples: shallow classifiers (SVMs, logistic regression), neural networks (MLPs, CNNs), deep unfolded model-based nets (learned AMP, DetNet), recurrent or sequence models (RNN/LSTM), and hybrid schemes that combine model-based algorithms with learned components.

Summarize empirical performance claims made for machine-learning-based MIMO detectors in non-Gaussian/impulsive noise environments: metrics where gains are reported (BER, SER, robustness to outliers, required SNR), typical operating regimes or noise parameters that show improvements, and any reported trade-offs (model complexity, training data dependence, generalization to different channel/noise conditions).
sub_answers.text: Machine-learning and learning-based approaches have been proposed alongside traditional signal-processing methods for CSI acquisition and related tasks in mmWave and massive MIMO systems [d59366s0p0]. Code-aided channel estimation schemes that jointly refine CSI and detection using coding constraints have demonstrated measurable performance gains in coded MIMO systems, with reported gains up to about 1.3 dB at a frame error rate of 10^{-4} for LDPC-coded QPSK in Rayleigh block-fading when compared to pilot-assisted transmission [d90654s0p0]. Comparisons of traditional versus machine learning-based CSI acquisition approaches consider metrics such as spectral efficiency, computational complexity, and overhead when evaluating potential benefits from learning-based methods [d59366s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: List the standard simulation setups, synthetic noise generators, and publicly available datasets/benchmarks used to assess detector robustness to impulsive noise: e.g., Middleton-class-A simulation parameters, alpha-stable noise sampling procedures, Bernoulli-Gaussian impulse models, channel models (i.i.d. Rayleigh, correlated MIMO, measured channels), plus any well-known open datasets or repositories used for reproducible comparisons and evaluation protocols (training/test splits, SNR ranges, BER/SER reporting).
sub_answers.text: Reproducible evaluations for MIMO algorithms commonly use simulation environments including ray-tracing-derived indoor channels for spatial channel variation studies [d5873s0p0]. Studies report standardized channel assumptions such as Rayleigh block-fading for performance evaluation and use standard modulations like QPSK together with standard codes such as WiMAX LDPC in simulations [d90654s0p0]. Evaluations distinguish narrowband and wideband system models and consider different receiver architectures (single versus multiple RF chains) and channel models including correlated and massive MIMO setups when assessing estimation and detection algorithms [d40825s0p0][d29878s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: In what ways do robust loss functions (e.g., Huber, Tukey’s biweight, redescending M-estimators) and explicit heavy-tailed likelihood families (alpha-stable laws, symmetric/asymmetric alpha-stable, generalized Gaussian, Student-t, compound Poisson, Gaussian mixture and contaminated Gaussian models) mathematically model impulsive noise, and how do they differ in representing impulsive event amplitude, impulsive occurrence rate, tail index, and skewness?
sub_answers.text:
Robust loss functions like the Huber likelihood bound the influence of large residuals by downweighting outliers through a piecewise loss that is quadratic near zero and linear in the tails, providing robustness to impulsive amplitudes [d82363s0p0][d38515s0p0].
Redescending M-estimators such as Tukey’s biweight further limit the influence of very large impulses by assigning zero weight beyond a cutoff, effectively truncating extreme amplitudes [d82363s0p0].
Heavy-tailed likelihood families model impulsive event amplitudes via fat-tailed density shapes and tail-index parameters (e.g., the alpha parameter in alpha-stable laws) that directly control tail heaviness and hence impulse magnitude statistics [d103127s0p0][d128145s0p0].
Compound models and shot-noise constructions represent impulsive occurrence rate explicitly by superposing random pulses or a Poisson shot-noise process, separating impulse occurrence statistics from per-impulse amplitude distributions [d128145s0p0][d103127s0p0].
Asymmetric or one-sided heavy-tailed families (e.g., positive tempered alpha-stable) capture skewness in impulse amplitudes by restricting support or introducing skew parameters, whereas symmetric families model zero-skew impulsive distributions [d103127s0p0][d128145s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which specific neural and hybrid architectures have been proposed for MIMO symbol detection — for example learned iterative algorithms and deep unfolding variants (DetNet, OAMP-Net/OAMP-Net2, LAMP, LISTA-style detectors), model-based deep unfolding for sphere-decoding, graph neural network detectors, convolutional/dilated CNNs, RNN/LSTM/GRU sequence models, autoencoder-based end-to-end receivers and residual networks — and what training strategies (supervised vs. self-supervised, curriculum learning, transfer learning, joint channel-and-symbol training, loss functions and data augmentation) are used to make them robust to interference and non-Gaussian noise?
sub_answers.text:
Loopy factor-graph receivers merge generalized approximate message passing (GAMP) with sequence decoding and turbo-style iterations to jointly estimate channel, impulses, symbols and bits in impulsive-noise OFDM, yielding near-optimal detection with O(N log N) complexity and parallelizability [d19014s0p0].
Learned iterative algorithms and deep-unfolding-style approaches are implemented by embedding GAMP-like message-passing within trainable modules and iterating with decoding, as in the proposed factor-graph-based receiver that attains performance close to matched-filter bounds [d19014s0p0].
Training strategies employed include soft-input soft-output decoding within a turbo loop and joint estimation of channel, noise impulses and symbols, effectively coupling model-based message passing with supervised symbol/bit-level objectives during receiver training [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What parameter-estimation approaches are used to infer unknown noise models and their hyperparameters from observed MIMO data — covering maximum likelihood and expectation-maximization for mixture and alpha-stable approximations, variational Bayes and collapsed VB, expectation propagation, MCMC and particle filters, method-of-moments and tail-index estimators (e.g., Hill, QQ-plot regression, Koutrouvelis’ method for alpha-stable), and robust estimation techniques (median-of-means, trimmed estimators) — and how do these methods handle identifiability, convergence and computational cost in practice?
sub_answers.text:
Characteristic-function-based parameter estimation is used to fit tempered alpha-stable compound-Gaussian amplitude models and extract texture parameters from clutter amplitudes [d103127s0p0].
Type-II maximum-likelihood (evidence) estimation is used to set hyperparameters in probabilistic models like Gaussian processes, providing a tractable empirical-Bayes approach to noise-model tuning [d82363s0p0].
Sparsity-aware adaptive algorithms such as normalized least-mean p-power (NLMP) variants with correntropy-induced metric penalties identify non-Gaussian impulsive systems by exploiting sparse structure while controlling impulsive-induced instability [d26508s0p0].
Joint estimation schemes based on factor-graph message passing (GAMP) enable practical convergence and computational tractability for large-tone problems by combining statistical estimation of channel and impulses with algorithmic scalability O(N log N) [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What kinds of feature engineering, input preprocessing and representation learning are effective at separating transmitted symbols from impulsive disturbances — including pilot-assisted and blind channel estimation schemes tailored for impulsive noise, robust pilot placement and interpolation, time-frequency transforms and wavelet denoising, kurtosis- and higher-order statistics-based detectors, rank-reduction/robust PCA and ICA, sparsity-based denoising and compressive sensing preprocessing, and learned denoisers (DnCNN, plug-and-play priors) applied before or within detectors?
sub_answers.text:
Group equivariant non-expansive operators (GENEOs) can control the expected perturbation of persistence diagrams and thus remove uniformly distributed impulsive noise in Lipschitz-function representations, providing a provable preprocessing for impulsive-noise removal [d74281s0p0].
Sparsity-exploiting preprocessing and adaptive NLMP algorithms leverage sparse structure in unknown systems to mitigate impulsive disturbances prior to detection [d26508s0p0].
Joint pilot-assisted channel-and-noise estimation embedded in factor-graph receivers separates symbol estimation from impulsive disturbances by concurrently estimating channel, noise impulses and symbols across OFDM tones [d19014s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What theoretical guarantees and asymptotic results exist on approximation power, consistency and robustness of neural network detectors under model mismatch or heavy-tailed noise — for example universal approximation theorems when noise has infinite variance, consistency and asymptotic normality of learned detectors under misspecified likelihoods, breakdown-point and influence-function analyses, minimax rates for detection/regression under heavy tails, and generalization bounds or robustness certificates for deep unfolding and end-to-end trained receivers?
sub_answers.text:
Adaptive Huber regression yields sharp phase-transition results and sub-Gaussian-type deviation bounds under heavy-tailed data when sufficient moments exist, establishing formal robustness and consistency regimes for estimators under heavy tails [d38515s0p0].
Robust Gaussian-process models with Huber likelihood use projection-statistic-based weighting to bound outlier influence and retain high statistical efficiency across Gaussian and thick-tailed noise distributions [d82363s0p0].
Compound Gaussian models with tempered alpha-stable texture admit explicit characteristic-function representations and scale-mixture amplitude forms, providing analytical structure for consistency and model-based inference under tunable tail behavior [d103127s0p0].
GENEO-based operators provide provable control of expected topological perturbation caused by impulsive noise, yielding theoretical stability guarantees for certain preprocessing operators in topological-data representations [d74281s0p0].
